summary: A 1971 Logger Protocol proposal by E. Meyer and T. Skinner. It was updated by RFC 123.

plainLanguage.summary: A proposal for rules for logging in to another computer.

questions: how did arpanet remote login work
what is a transaction block in the logger protocol
subtitle: An early proposal for how a user on one ARPANET host could log in to another host over the network.

tldr.problem: With the Host-to-Host Protocol specified, the authors wanted a common way to log in to a remote host from a console, instead of each of some 20 hosts defining its own.
tldr.mechanism: The login uses the NCP connection steps of RFC 80, then a dialog of ASCII text messages sent as transaction blocks that each carry a code byte, a count byte and up to 127 characters.
tldr.outcome: Only the login mechanism is covered. What happens after login is left to each site's own experiments. The RFC was later updated by RFC 123.

today: RFC 98 was updated by RFC 123. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown, and the RFC itself is a proposal for discussion.

sections.title: Why a Logger Protocol
sections.content:
A logger is the mechanism that lets a user log in to a system from a console. A network logger specifies how a host's existing logger interfaces to the network so that a user at a console attached to another host can log in. The authors, at project MAC, noted a widespread feeling that this should be the first step after the Host-to-Host Protocol.

They give two reasons: users want direct experience of remote systems, and remote login is probably less complex than tasks like generalized file transfer. They also reject letting each host set its own approach: interfacing with some 20 systems would be more time-consuming than interfacing with one, and a common protocol fosters a sense of network community.

This proposal covers only login. A login has three phases: connection, dialog (identifying the user and verifying their right to use the system, which may be minimal), and admission (switching the user's connections from the logger to a command processor).
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every computer inventing its own doorbell, this proposes one doorbell that works everywhere.

sections.title: The Connection Phase
sections.content:
The RFC endorses the connection scheme of RFC 80 and restates it. The using host's NCP sends a request for connection (RTS) from the user's receive socket to the serving host's logger contact socket, whose 24-bit user number field is zero. The serving host may refuse with a close (CLS), or accept by sending STR and then immediately closing, which frees the contact socket. The logger then picks two sockets and sends connection requests to the user's sockets. If the user accepts within a reasonable time, the connection phase is over; if not, the requests are aborted.

A logger should disconnect when it abandons a login or the user logs out, or when it receives a close or a network error message. Disconnecting stops any activity for that user: an unfinished login is abandoned and a logged-in user's process is stopped, though absentee jobs are not meant to be restricted.
sections.plainLanguage: The visitor knocks, the host says 'come to a different door', and then the host opens two new doors, one to talk and one to listen.

sections.title: Dialog and Transaction Blocks
sections.content:
Each host may define its own login dialog (names, projects, passwords) as long as it fits a sequence of messages. The host chooses whether the logger or the user speaks first. Text is standard ASCII, and each host must map its own character set to ASCII and back unambiguously. The only standard end of a console line is the line feed character (012), and a character with no ASCII equivalent can be sent as ESC (033) plus another ASCII character.

Messages are sent as transaction blocks: <code> <count> <char1> ... <charn>, each element 8 bits with the top bit zero. Here code is zero, count ranges from 0 to 127, and a block holds at most 127 characters. The count lets systems without per-character scanning wait for the whole block. A message must start and end on block boundaries, and two messages cannot share a block. The first 8 bits sent on a new connection are a type code from Protocol Document 1, which the receiver discards.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note starts with a number saying how many letters follow, so the reader knows how much to read before it stops.

sections.title: Other Issues Raised
sections.content:
The RFC raises several points without demanding firm agreement. There is no network echoplex option for login: a using system in echoplex mode must echo locally, and a serving system should suppress the echo of input during login. Typing mistakes are fixed by the editing conventions of either host, and an unfixable mistake means aborting the login by closing a connection and starting over.

A logger should not wait forever for a reply, and should abort after a reasonable interval (perhaps a minute). In this initial scheme, socket ownership cannot follow administratively assigned user codes because the logger assigns sockets before the user is verified. A future protocol could transfer the connections to the user's sockets during admission. A companion paper on general console communications was in preparation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you type something wrong, start over. If you wait too long at the door, the host closes it. Other details were left for later.
